# Module 1 — Full Test Bank {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note}
## How this test bank works
This bank holds **20 questions**: five in each of four sections. On the real test you receive **four questions — one from each section** — and you submit an `.xlsx` workbook with **a separate sheet for each section's answers**. Each question is designed to take about **8–10 minutes**.

Expand each **Answer** block to check your work. Every value has been computed from the real data; when the source files are refreshed the exact numbers may shift slightly, but the method stays the same.
:::

**The three datasets.**

- **Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields** (1990–2025). Average yield (bu/ac) for eight crops in every Rural Municipality. Wide file `rm_yields_1990plus.csv` for Sections 2–3; long file `rm_yields_1990plus_long.csv` for Section 4. Blank = crop not grown/reported that RM-year.
- **Manitoba Wheat Variety** (2020–2025). Red spring wheat yield by variety and municipality. `Reported = FALSE` marks a yield **suppressed** by MASC because too few farms grew that variety there.
- **Canada Field Crops** (StatsCan, 2015–2025). Seeded acres and average yield (bu/ac) for major field crops, by province.

**Grading model.** Visual appearance **20%**, plus **20%** for each of the four sections (Building a Worksheet, Descriptive, Conditional, PivotTables) = 100%. Histograms and PivotTables are marked partly on how clearly they are presented — titles, axis labels, formatting.

> **Vocabulary note.** Everything here uses only Module 1 tools: mean/median/mode, range, IQR, variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, percentiles/quartiles, symmetric vs skewed shape, outliers (the 1.5×IQR rule), histograms, relative and absolute references, number and date formatting, `ROUND`, and PivotTables.

---

# Section 1 — Building a Worksheet

*These questions are about spreadsheet mechanics: anchoring references, formatting numbers and dates, and order of operations. The data is given in the question — copy the block and paste it into Excel.*

### Question 1

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Field	Acres	Yield (bu/ac)
North	120	41.2
South	240	38.6
Creek	95	44.8
Home	310	36.1
Rented	175	39.9
```

Above the table, put the canola price **$14.20** in a single labelled cell.

**(a)** Add a **Revenue ($/ac)** column: each field's yield times the price cell. Write the formula once and fill it down. Format as currency with two decimals.

**(b)** Add a **Total revenue ($)** column: revenue per acre times that field's acres. Format with a thousands separator and no decimals.

**(c)** Under the table, use `SUM` to total the acres and the total revenue.

**(d)** In a spare cell, write the version of the (a) formula *without* the `$` signs and fill it down two rows, labelled clearly as the incorrect version.

**(e)** In one sentence beside it, say what a reader would see in that column and why.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=C2*$B$1` (wherever the price sits) → $585.04, $548.12, $636.16, $512.62, $566.58.
- (b) `=D2*B2` → $70,204.80 · $131,548.80 · $60,435.20 · $158,912.20 · $99,151.50.
- (c) Acres **940**; total revenue **$520,252.50**.
- (d) `=C2*B1` filled down.
- (e) Every row after the first returns $0.00, because the reference walks down to empty cells. Excel reports no error.
</details>

### Question 2

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Field	Canola	Wheat	Barley
North	41.2	52.4	63.1
South	38.6	49.8	58.7
Creek	44.8	55.2	66.4
Home	36.1	47.3	61.9
Rented	39.9	51.0	60.2
```

Directly above the three yield columns, enter the prices in a single row: Canola **$14.20**, Wheat **$8.35**, Barley **$5.60**.

**(a)** To the right, build a revenue-per-acre block of the same shape. Write **one** formula in its top-left cell and fill it across and down to complete all fifteen cells.

**(b)** State the formula you used, and say which part of the price reference is locked and which is not.

**(c)** Under your revenue block, use `AVERAGE` to find the mean revenue per acre for each crop.

**(d)** Which crop gives the highest average revenue per acre, and by how much over the second-placed crop?

**(e)** A student anchors the price fully as `$B$1` instead. In one sentence, say what their wheat and barley columns would show and why nothing on the sheet would look broken.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=B2*B$1` filled across and down.
- (b) Only the **row** is locked. Filling down must keep pointing at row 1; filling across must let the column move so each crop meets its own price.
- (c) Canola **$569.70**, Wheat **$427.02**, Barley **$347.54**.
- (d) **Canola**, by **$142.68** over wheat.
- (e) Every column would use the canola price, so wheat and barley revenues would be roughly 70% and 150% too high. The sheet still fills with plausible dollar figures, so nothing signals the error.
</details>

### Question 3

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Date	Crop	Tonnes
14 September 2026	Canola	42.5
18 September 2026	Canola	38.0
23 September 2026	Wheat	61.2
2 October 2026	Wheat	55.8
9 October 2026	Barley	47.3
```

**(a)** Make sure Excel has read the dates as **dates**, not text, and format them `DD-Mon-YYYY`. Show tonnes to one decimal.

**(b)** Add a **Days since previous** column. Leave the first row blank. Make sure the results show as plain numbers.

**(c)** In one cell, compute the number of days from the first delivery to the last.

**(d)** Use `SUM` to total the tonnes, and `AVERAGE` to find the mean load size.

**(e)** In one sentence, explain how you can tell by looking at a cell whether Excel read a date as a date or as text, and why it matters for part (b).

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Dates formatted `DD-MMM-YYYY`; tonnes `0.0`.
- (b) `=A3-A2` filled down → **4, 5, 9, 7** days. If the cell shows `04-Jan-1900` it inherited the date format; change it to Number.
- (c) `=A6-A2` = **25** days.
- (d) Total **244.8** tonnes; mean **48.96** tonnes.
- (e) A real date is right-aligned by default; text is left-aligned. Text dates cannot be subtracted, so (b) would fail.
</details>

### Question 4

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Load	Protein
A	0.1342
B	0.1285
C	0.1401
D	0.1198
E	0.1356
```

**(a)** Copy the protein column into three further columns so the same five numbers appear four times. Format them, one column each, as: General, Number with 2 decimals, Percentage with 1 decimal, and Percentage with 2 decimals. Label each column with the format used.

**(b)** Under every column, compute the average with `AVERAGE`.

**(c)** The four averages display differently but hold the same number. In a spare cell, write that value to four decimal places.

**(d)** The contract pays a premium on any load above 13.5% protein. Add a column using `IF` that returns `Yes` or `No`, and use `COUNTIF` to count how many qualify.

**(e)** A student writes `=IF(B2>13.5,"Yes","No")` and gets `No` for every load. In one sentence, explain the error.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Same five values throughout; only the format differs.
- (b) All four averages hold the same number, displaying as `0.1316`, `0.13`, `13.2%`, `13.16%`.
- (c) **0.1316**.
- (d) `=IF(B2>0.135,"Yes","No")`; `=COUNTIF(D2:D6,"Yes")` = **2** (loads C and E).
- (e) The cells hold proportions, not percentages — 0.1342, not 13.42. Nothing is above 13.5, so every row returns `No`. Formatting a cell as a percentage does not change the stored value.
</details>

### Question 5

*Paste this block into a blank sheet.*

```{.plain}
Bin	Crop	Price ($/bu)	Bushels
1	Canola	14.20	2400
2	Wheat	8.35	5100
3	Barley	5.60	3800
```

**(a)** Add a **Value ($)** column and total it with `SUM`. Format as currency.

**(b)** Should the price reference be absolute here? Answer in one sentence and say why.

**(c)** In three spare cells below, write the version that anchors the price as `$C$2`, fill it down all three rows, and total it. Label the block as the incorrect version.

**(d)** State the difference between the two totals and which crop's price the incorrect version applied to every bin.

**(e)** A buyer offers a flat **$0.30/bu** premium on everything in storage. Put the premium in one labelled cell and add a **Value with premium** column that all three rows point at. Explain in one sentence why *this* reference must be absolute when the price one must not.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=C2*D2` → $34,080 · $42,585 · $21,280. Total **$97,945.00**.
- (b) **No.** Each row has its own price, so the reference must move with the row.
- (c) `=$C$2*D2` → $34,080 · $72,420 · $53,960; total **$160,460**.
- (d) **$62,515** too high. It applies the **canola** price of $14.20 to every bin.
- (e) `=(C2+$F$1)*D2` → total **$101,335.00**. The premium sits in one cell every row must reach, so it must be anchored; the price sits on each row, so it must not be.
</details>

# Section 2 — Descriptive Statistics and Distributions

*These questions use the **Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields** dataset (`rm_yields_1990plus.csv`): average yield in bushels per acre for each crop in every Rural Municipality. A blank cell means that crop was not grown or not reported in that RM that year.*

### Question 6

Filter the data to `Year = 2023` and work with the **Canola** column.

**(a)** Compute the mean and the median canola yield.

**(b)** The two differ. State which is larger and, in one or two sentences, say what that tells you about how the low-yielding RMs are distributed.

**(c)** Compute the standard deviation and the coefficient of variation.

**(d)** Repeat (a) and (c) for the **Barley** column in the same year.

**(e)** Barley's standard deviation is much larger than canola's. Using your CVs, explain in two sentences whether barley yields were genuinely more variable, and why comparing the raw standard deviations alone would mislead.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Mean **33.88**, median **35.50** bu/ac (n = 289).
- (b) The mean is **below** the median, so a minority of RMs with unusually low yields — down to 3.4 bu/ac — pull the average beneath the middle value. Most RMs sit higher than the mean suggests.
- (c) SD **13.33**; CV = 13.33 / 33.88 = **0.394**.
- (d) Barley: mean **54.56**, SD **24.60**, CV **0.451**.
- (e) Barley's SD is nearly twice canola's, but barley also yields far more per acre, so part of that spread is just scale. The CVs (0.451 vs 0.394) show barley was only modestly more variable *relative to its own average*. Comparing raw SDs across crops with different means overstates the difference.
</details>

### Question 7

Filter to `Year = 2023`, **Spring Wheat** column.

**(a)** Compute the first and third quartiles with `QUARTILE.INC`, and the interquartile range.

**(b)** Compute the 10th and 90th percentiles with `PERCENTILE.INC`.

**(c)** In one sentence, say what the 10th percentile means for a farmer in this dataset.

**(d)** Compute the range (`MAX` − `MIN`).

**(e)** The range is far larger than the IQR. Explain in two sentences why, and say which of the two you would quote in a report describing a typical spread across RMs.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Q1 **28.50**, Q3 **55.60**, IQR **27.10** bu/ac.
- (b) 10th percentile **19.34**, 90th percentile **64.92** bu/ac.
- (c) One RM in ten had an average spring wheat yield at or below 19.34 bu/ac that year.
- (d) 74.7 − 5.0 = **69.70** bu/ac.
- (e) The range is set entirely by the two most extreme RMs, so a single failed or exceptional RM defines it. The IQR covers the middle half and ignores both tails, so it is the better description of a typical spread — quote the IQR, and mention the extremes separately if they matter.
</details>

### Question 8

Filter to `Year = 2023`, **Canola** column.

**(a)** Build a histogram of the canola yields with about 10–15 bins. Give it a descriptive title and label both axes.

**(b)** Describe the shape in one or two sentences: symmetric, or skewed — and if skewed, in which direction.

**(c)** Compute the mean and median again and mark both on your chart or state them beneath it.

**(d)** Explain in one sentence how the position of the mean relative to the median matches the shape you described in (b).

**(e)** A classmate makes the same histogram with 3 bins and concludes the data is symmetric. In one or two sentences, explain what went wrong.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Histogram, 10–15 bins, titled and labelled.
- (b) **Left-skewed** (a tail toward the low yields): most RMs cluster between roughly 25 and 50 bu/ac, with a thin tail running down toward 3.4.
- (c) Mean **33.88**, median **35.50**.
- (d) The mean sits below the median, which is what a low tail does — the extreme low values pull the average down while the middle value barely moves.
- (e) Three bins are too coarse to show the tail. Each bin spans about 19 bu/ac, so the low RMs get absorbed into a wide left-hand bar and the asymmetry disappears. Bin width has to be fine enough to reveal the shape without showing random noise.
</details>

### Question 9

Filter to `Year = 2023`. You will use the **Canola** and **Barley** columns.

**(a)** Compute the mean of each, along with the mean of the **Oats** column.

**(b)** Use `COUNT` on each of the three columns. The three counts differ. In one sentence, say what that difference tells you about the dataset.

**(c)** Explain in one sentence why `COUNT` and `COUNTA` would give different answers if the blank cells contained the text `"n/a"` instead of being empty.

**(d)** A student fills every blank canola cell with 0 and recomputes the mean. Compute what that mean would be, and state the difference from your answer in (a).

**(e)** In two sentences, explain why filling blanks with zero is wrong here, and what the blank actually represents.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola **33.88**, Barley **54.56**, Oats **71.14**.
- (b) Canola 289, Barley 285, Oats 200. Not every crop is grown or reported in every RM, so the columns have different numbers of observations.
- (c) `COUNT` counts numbers only, so it would still return 289; `COUNTA` counts any non-empty cell, so it would also count the `"n/a"` entries and return 295 — the full number of 2023 rows.
- (d) With 295 rows and six zeros, the mean falls to **33.19** — about **0.69** bu/ac lower.
- (e) A blank means the crop was not grown or not reported, not that the RM harvested nothing. Entering 0 turns a missing observation into a measured failure and drags the average down.
</details>

### Question 10

Using the whole dataset (all years), work with the **Canola** column.

**(a)** Compute the mean canola yield for `Year = 2021` and for `Year = 2022`.

**(b)** Compute the percentage change from 2021 to 2022 and format it as a percentage with one decimal.

**(c)** State the formula you used and say which year belongs in the denominator, and why.

**(d)** Compute the standard deviation for each of the two years.

**(e)** In two sentences, use both the means and the standard deviations to describe what happened between the two years. Say what a single mean on its own would have hidden.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) 2021 mean **21.86**, 2022 mean **35.40** bu/ac.
- (b) `=(B2-B1)/B1` = **+61.9%**.
- (c) The **starting** year (2021) goes in the denominator: percentage change measures movement relative to where you began.
- (d) 2021 SD **8.14**; 2022 SD **12.38**.
- (e) Average yields rose by about three-fifths after the 2021 drought, and the spread widened as well — RMs did not all recover equally. A mean alone would have shown the recovery but hidden the fact that the gap between good and poor RMs grew.
</details>

# Section 3 — Conditional Functions & Lookups

*These questions use the **Saskatchewan RM Crop Yields** dataset (`rm_yields_1990plus.csv`).*

### Question 11

Filter to `Year = 2023`.

**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` to count the RMs with a canola yield above 40 bu/ac.

**(b)** Use `COUNTIF` to count those at or below 20 bu/ac.

**(c)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to find the mean **barley** yield in those RMs where canola came in above 40.

**(d)** Compute the mean barley yield across all RMs in 2023, and compare it with your answer to (c).

**(e)** In two sentences, say what the comparison suggests, and give one reason other than crop choice that might explain it.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=COUNTIF(C2:C290,">40")` = **114** RMs.
- (b) `=COUNTIF(C2:C290,"<=20")` = **57** RMs.
- (c) `=AVERAGEIF(C2:C290,">40",D2:D290)` = **77.40** bu/ac.
- (d) All-RM barley mean **54.56**; the good-canola RMs averaged **22.84** bu/ac more.
- (e) RMs that grew canola well also grew barley well, which points to something affecting both crops rather than to the crops themselves. Growing-season rainfall is the obvious candidate — soil zone and seeding date would also do it.
</details>

### Question 12

Filter to `Year = 2023`.

**(a)** Use `IF` to add a column labelling each RM `Above` or `Below` according to whether its canola yield beats the 2023 canola mean. Compute the mean in its own cell and point the `IF` at that cell.

**(b)** Use `COUNTIF` to count how many RMs fall in each category.

**(c)** The two counts are not equal. In one or two sentences, explain what that tells you about the distribution.

**(d)** Now repeat (a) and (b) using the **median** instead of the mean.

**(e)** The median split is much closer to even. In two sentences, explain why that is guaranteed by the definition of the median, and what the mean split told you that the median split did not.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=IF(C2>$G$1,"Above","Below")` where `G1` holds `=AVERAGE(C2:C290)` = 33.88.
- (b) Above **153**, Below **136**.
- (c) More RMs sit above the mean than below it (153 to 136), which is the signature of a low tail: a minority of very poor RMs drags the mean down past the middle of the data.
- (d) Median 35.50 → Above **143**, Below **146**.
- (e) The median is *defined* as the value with half the observations on each side, so the split is even by construction (143/146, the difference being ties at the median). The mean split is informative precisely because it is uneven — the 153/136 gap is a measure of the skew that the median split cannot show.
</details>

### Question 13

Filter to `Year = 2023`. Build a small price table somewhere on your sheet:

```{.plain}
Crop	Price ($/bu)
Canola	14.20
Spring Wheat	8.35
Barley	5.60
Oats	4.50
```

**(a)** Use `XLOOKUP` to pull the canola price into a cell, looking it up by name rather than typing the number.

**(b)** Add a **Canola revenue ($/ac)** column: each RM's canola yield times the looked-up price. Write it once and fill it down.

**(c)** Explain in one sentence which references in your formula had to be absolute.

**(d)** Use `AVERAGE` to find the mean canola revenue per acre across RMs, and `MAX` to find the highest.

**(e)** Change the canola price in your price table to **$11.50**. State what happens to your revenue column, and explain in one sentence why this is better practice than typing 14.20 into the formula.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=XLOOKUP("Canola",$F$2:$F$5,$G$2:$G$5)` = 14.20.
- (b) `=C2*$H$1` where `H1` holds the looked-up price.
- (c) The lookup ranges (`$F$2:$F$5`, `$G$2:$G$5`) and the price cell (`$H$1`) — all must stay put as the formula fills down.
- (d) Mean **$481.11**/ac; maximum **$853.42**/ac.
- (e) Every revenue updates at once. The price lives in one place, so it can be checked, sourced and changed without editing 289 formulas — and there is no risk of a stale number hiding inside a formula.
</details>

### Question 14

Filter to `Year = 2023`.

**(a)** Use `SUMIF` to total the canola yields of RMs with a canola yield above 40 bu/ac.

**(b)** Use `COUNTIF` to count those RMs, then divide to get their mean.

**(c)** Check your answer to (b) using `AVERAGEIF`. The two should match.

**(d)** In one sentence, say when you would prefer `SUMIF` and `COUNTIF` over `AVERAGEIF`.

**(e)** A student writes `=COUNTIF(C2:C290,">AVERAGE(C2:C290)")` to count RMs above the mean, and gets 0. Explain the error in one or two sentences and give the formula that works.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) `=SUMIF(C2:C290,">40")` = **5,399.60**.
- (b) 5,399.60 / 114 = **47.36** bu/ac.
- (c) `=AVERAGEIF(C2:C290,">40")` = **47.36** — the same.
- (d) When you need the total as well as the average, or when the criterion range and the averaging range differ in a way that is easier to write out in two steps.
- (e) Everything inside quotation marks is treated as literal text, so Excel searches for cells containing the characters `>AVERAGE(...)` and finds none. Join the operator to the computed value instead: `=COUNTIF(C2:C290,">"&AVERAGE(C2:C290))` = **153**.
</details>

### Question 15

Filter to `Year = 2023`.

**(a)** Use `COUNTIF` twice to count the RMs whose **canola** yield is above 40, and the RMs whose **barley** yield is above 70.

**(b)** Use `AVERAGEIF` to find the mean canola yield in RMs where **barley** came in above 70 bu/ac. Note carefully which column is tested and which is averaged.

**(c)** Compare that with the overall mean canola yield and state the difference.

**(d)** Add an `IF` column flagging RMs where canola is above 40 **and** barley is above 70, returning `Both` or a blank. (`IF` alone is enough — nest a second `IF` inside the first.)

**(e)** Count the `Both` RMs with `COUNTIF`, and in two sentences say what the number suggests about whether good canola RMs and good barley RMs are the same places.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Canola above 40: **114**. Barley above 70: **96**.
- (b) `=AVERAGEIF(D2:D290,">70",C2:C290)` = **46.60** bu/ac — testing barley, averaging canola.
- (c) The overall canola mean is 33.88, so RMs with strong barley averaged **12.72** bu/ac more canola.
- (d) `=IF(C2>40,IF(D2>70,"Both",""),"")`.
- (e) **86** RMs qualify on both counts. That is most of the 96 strong-barley RMs, so good canola and good barley land in largely the same places — consistent with a shared cause such as rainfall rather than anything specific to either crop.
</details>

# Section 4 — PivotTables

*These questions use the **long** version of the Saskatchewan RM data (`rm_yields_1990plus_long.csv`), with one row per RM-year-crop. A PivotTable can only group by a field that lives in its own column, which is why the long shape is needed here.*

### Question 16

**(a)** Build a PivotTable with **Crop** in Rows and average **Yield** in Values. Change the summary from Sum to **Average**.

**(b)** One crop shows an average in the hundreds while the rest are in the tens. Name it and explain in one sentence what has gone wrong with the comparison.

**(c)** Add **Year** to Columns and filter to 2021–2023.

**(d)** Read off the average canola yield in each of those three years.

**(e)** In two sentences, describe what happened to canola between 2021 and 2023, and say what the Crop-only table in (a) hid.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Crop in Rows, Yield in Values, set to Average.
- (b) **Lentils**, averaging about **1,208**. Lentils are reported in **pounds** per acre while every other crop is in bushels per acre, so the column mixes two units and the averages cannot be compared. The `Unit` column in the long file records which is which.
- (c) Year in Columns, filtered to 2021–2023.
- (d) Canola: 2021 **21.86**, 2022 **35.40**, 2023 **33.88** bu/ac.
- (e) Canola yields collapsed in the 2021 drought and rose about 62% the following year, holding near that level in 2023. A single all-years average of about 28 bu/ac would have hidden a swing of that size entirely.
</details>

### Question 17

**(a)** Build a PivotTable of average **Yield** by **Year**, filtered to the **Canola** crop only.

**(b)** Identify the three worst years and the three best, with their averages.

**(c)** Change the summary from Average to **Count**. What is the count telling you, and why does it vary by year?

**(d)** Switch back to Average and add **Count** as a second Values field so both appear side by side.

**(e)** One year has a noticeably lower count than its neighbours. In two sentences, explain why a low count should make you more cautious about that year's average.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Year in Rows, Yield in Values set to Average, Crop filtered to Canola.
- (b) Worst: **2002** (15.83), **2003** (17.03), **2001** (18.19). Best: **2025** (43.94), **2016** (42.18), **2019** (40.78).
- (c) The count is the number of RMs reporting a canola yield that year. It varies because not every RM grows canola every year, and because reporting coverage changes over time.
- (d) Both fields in Values: Average of Yield and Count of Yield.
- (e) An average computed from few RMs is more sensitive to any single unusual RM, so it is a less reliable summary of the province. It may also reflect a different set of RMs than other years, so year-to-year comparisons are not quite like for like.
</details>

### Question 18

**(a)** Build a PivotTable with **Year** in Rows and **Crop** in Columns, showing average **Yield**.

**(b)** Filter to the years 2019–2023 and to Canola, Spring Wheat and Barley.

**(c)** Read off the 2021 row. All three crops are low. What does that pattern suggest about the cause?

**(d)** Compute, for each of the three crops, how much its 2022 average exceeded its 2021 average.

**(e)** In two sentences, say which crop recovered most in absolute terms and which recovered most in proportional terms, and explain why the two answers differ.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Year in Rows, Crop in Columns, Average of Yield in Values.
- (b) Filtered to 2019–2023 and the three crops.
- (c) All three crops fell together, which points to a cause affecting the whole growing season rather than anything crop-specific — the 2021 drought.
- (d) Canola **+13.54** (21.86 → 35.40), Spring Wheat **+15.58** (30.22 → 45.80), Barley **+26.50** (34.83 → 61.33).
- (e) **Barley** recovered most in absolute terms (+26.50 bu/ac) *and* proportionally (+76%, against canola's +62% and wheat's +52%). Barley yields far more per acre to begin with, so its absolute gain would be largest even at an equal percentage — check both before claiming one crop recovered the most.
</details>

### Question 19

**(a)** Build a PivotTable of average **Yield** by **Crop**, with **Year** as a Filter (not in Rows or Columns).

**(b)** Set the filter to 2021 and record the averages for all crops.

**(c)** Set it to 2022 and record them again.

**(d)** Which crop showed the largest proportional improvement between the two years?

**(e)** In two sentences, explain the difference between putting Year in the **Filter** area and putting it in **Columns**, and say when you would choose each.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Crop in Rows, Yield in Values set to Average, Year in Filters.

### Question 20

**(a)** Build a PivotTable with **Crop** in Rows and average **Yield** in Values, filtered to `Year = 2023`.

**(b)** Add **Count** of Yield alongside the average.

**(c)** Two crops have far fewer observations than the rest. Name them and give their counts.

**(d)** Compute the same two averages a second way, using `AVERAGEIF` on the long file directly, and confirm they match your PivotTable.

**(e)** In two sentences, say why it is worth checking a PivotTable result against a formula at least once, and what kind of mistake this catches.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

- (a) Crop in Rows, Average of Yield, filtered to 2023.
- (b) Both fields in Values.
- (c) **Flax** (**164**) and **Durum** (**173**), against 285–289 for canola, wheat and barley.
- (d) `=AVERAGEIF(crop_range,"Flax",yield_range)` = **20.31**, and the same for Durum = **29.60** — both match the PivotTable.
- (e) A PivotTable silently applies whatever filters are set, and it is easy to leave one on from an earlier step or to summarise the wrong field. Recomputing one figure with a formula catches exactly that kind of error, which produces a plausible-looking number rather than an error message.
</details>
